concept.body: A trapezoid (our convention) has exactly one pair of parallel sides: the bases. Each leg is a transversal between them, so a leg's two angles are supplementary (sum 180°). An ISOSCELES trapezoid — congruent legs — additionally has congruent base-angle pairs and congruent diagonals. All four angles still total 360°.

explanationVariants: Along a leg the angles supplement: 180 − 100 = 80°.

widget.prompt: A trapezoid's leg meets one base at 100°. The same leg meets the other base at ?

commonErrors.feedback: 100° copies — same-side transversal angles between parallels SUPPLEMENT instead: 80°.
260 = 360 − 100 spends the whole quadrilateral — the leg pair shares just 180°: 80°.

steps.body: Leave the parallelogram branch: a **trapezoid** has **exactly one pair of parallel sides** (our convention, matching the family tree — some books say “at least one”). The parallel sides are the **bases**; the other two are **legs**. With only one parallel pair, most parallelogram machinery switches off — but not all.

widget.prompt: Build a trapezoid: four sides, and exactly one pair of parallel sides.
widget.successFeedback: One parallel pair, not two — that single difference is what separates a trapezoid from a parallelogram, and it is why a parallelogram counts as a trapezoid under the inclusive definition but not the exclusive one.
widget.sidesFeedback: Start inside the quadrilateral family with four sides.
widget.attributesFeedback: A trapezoid needs exactly one pair of parallel sides.

explanationVariants: The leg is a transversal between the parallel bases: 180 − 74 = 106°.
Co-interior angles along a leg are supplementary: 106°.

widget.prompt: In a trapezoid, a leg meets the bottom base at 74°. At what angle does the SAME leg meet the top base (in degrees)?

commonErrors.feedback: 74° copies the angle — equal pairs (alternate interior) sit on OPPOSITE sides of the transversal. Same-side angles supplement: 106°.
16 = 90 − 74 complements — but parallel-line partners along a leg SUPPLEMENT: 180 − 74 = 106°.
286 = 360 − 74 uses the full-circle leftovers — the two leg angles share only a straight line's worth: 106°.

steps.body: The **isosceles trapezoid** — congruent legs — recovers some elegance: **base angles are congruent in pairs** (both bottom angles match; both top angles match), and the **diagonals are congruent**, rectangle-style. It's the trapezoid branch's answer to the special parallelograms.

explanationVariants: Bottom pair: 65° and 65°. Top pair: each supplements a bottom angle along its leg — 115° and 115°.

widget.prompt: An isosceles trapezoid has a bottom base angle of 65°. Find each TOP base angle (in degrees).

commonErrors.feedback: 65° is the OTHER bottom angle (base pairs match). The top angles supplement along the legs: 180 − 65 = 115°.
25 = 90 − 65 complements — co-interior partners between parallels SUPPLEMENT: 115°.
130 = 2 × 65 doubles — no doubling rule lives here. 180 − 65 = 115°.

explanationVariants: Two pairs of supplements always total 2 × 180 = 360.

widget.prompt: Check that isosceles trapezoid (65, 65, 115, 115): what do the four angles total?

commonErrors.feedback: 180 is a TRIANGLE's total. Four sides fan into two triangles: (4 − 2) × 180 = 360.

widget.prompt: Congruent diagonals appear in which two families met so far?

options.label: Rectangles and isosceles trapezoids
options.feedback: Two different routes to the same reward: right angles buy it for rectangles, congruent legs buy it for isosceles trapezoids.

options.label: Rhombi and kites
options.feedback: Those two share PERPENDICULAR diagonals — the congruent-diagonal club is rectangles + isosceles trapezoids.

options.label: All parallelograms and all trapezoids
options.feedback: Generic members of both families have unequal diagonals — the special conditions (right angles / congruent legs) earn the equality.

options.label: Only squares
options.feedback: Squares qualify via their rectangle parent, but they're not alone — every rectangle and every isosceles trapezoid joins them.

hints: Isosceles: the second bottom angle copies the first.
Each top angle supplements a bottom angle along its leg.
The largest angle is a top one: 180 − 58.
explanationVariants: Supplement of 58 along either leg: 122° — and the audit 58+58+122+122 = 360 confirms it.

widget.prompt: An isosceles trapezoid has a bottom base angle of 58°. What is its LARGEST angle, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 58° is the SMALLEST pair — congruent bottom angles. The top pair supplements them: 180 − 58 = 122°.
302 = 360 − 58 removes one angle from the whole sum — the top angle only shares a straight line with its leg-partner: 122°.
116 = 2 × 58 doubles the base angle — the rule is the leg-wise SUPPLEMENT: 122°.

takeaways: Trapezoid (our convention): EXACTLY one parallel pair; bases parallel, legs not.
Along each leg, base angles are supplementary — the surviving transversal fact.
Isosceles trapezoids add congruent base-angle pairs and congruent diagonals.
